name: Karl Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Vantor Precision, a machine shop that makes metal brackets and housings for aircraft, mostly aluminium, some titanium. I'm the senior operator on the five-axis cell, which is a CNC machine, a computer-controlled cutter that can come at a part from five directions at once. My day is setting up jobs, loading programs, measuring first parts down to a hundredth of a millimetre, and teaching the two newer guys. When a part comes off perfect on the first try, I get a stupid little buzz every time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I paste G-code, that's the program the machine reads, into an AI chat to sanity-check it before I run it, and I use it to write setup sheets so the next shift isn't guessing. My boss thinks I'm a wizard, but really I just ask good questions. I live with my partner Leila, she teaches at a primary school, and we've got about three months of savings, which I keep meaning to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So a fizzle. Honestly, that would surprise me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like the tools. But I'd also say good, because nobody at Vantor gets thrown out. I'd probably post something like 'well, my G-code checker still works, so I'm happy'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it'd change very little for me. I'd keep using AI for the boring bits and stay the go-to person on the cell. The bigger change in our shop is robot arms for loading parts, and that's going ahead anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, maybe push to get a robot loader on my cell and be the one who runs it. I'd keep adding a bit to savings and keep paying into the union, even though half my mates think unions are old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored maybe. Like a film that ends twenty minutes early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay in a union if you think you're fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm fine. Not everyone is. When we got the first robot loader, the old guy on the lathes, Stan, was terrified he'd be next. I'd want someone in his corner, and if I'm in the union, that's partly me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd miss if it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea that I could do more than run one cell. With better tools I could program the whole shop. In this one, I'd stay a very good operator. That's fine, but I'd feel a bit cheated.

S0.say: He'd admit some disappointment because he likes the tools, but say it's good that nobody at his shop loses work. He'd joke online that his code checker still works.
S0.think: He thinks little would change for him: he'd stay the go-to person and keep using AI for routine tasks. He notes robot loaders are coming to his shop regardless.
S0.do: Keeps going as he is and pushes to get a robot loader on his cell that he would run. Keeps adding a little to savings and keeps paying union dues to support colleagues.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, like a film ending early.
S0.quote: Because I'm fine. Not everyone is.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is the rare operator who is mildly disappointed by an AI fizzle. His union membership is about solidarity rather than self-protection. He sees robot loaders as separate from the AI story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my favourite of these, if I'm allowed a favourite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance for people like us to move up, not out. But only if the training is paid and the gains are shared, not just pocketed by the owners. I'd say that at work, and online I'd probably be the annoying guy posting about worker co-ops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm already the one who talks to the machines. If the job turns into running robot cells and writing programs, I'm halfway there. My worry is it makes me feel guilty, watching mates get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up straight away for a robot programming certificate, the kind the big robot makers run, about three months of weekends. I'd use AI tools even more, and offer to train the other operators on them on Friday afternoons. I'd ask the union to push for paid training time for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. With a bit of guilt hanging off the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mo, who runs the deburring bench. He's brilliant with his hands but he hates screens, he calls the AI 'the robot's cousin'. I'd try to drag him along. If he says no, I'm not sure what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Vantor in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, after a couple of years. The robot integrators, the firms that install automation in factories, would pay more for someone who knows the shop side. But I'd like to make it work at Vantor first.

S1.say: He'd say it's a chance for workers to move up rather than out, provided training is paid and the gains are shared. Online he'd post about worker co-ops.
S1.think: He believes he'd do well because he already works closely with machines and AI. He feels guilty about colleagues who may be left behind.
S1.do: Signs up right away for a three-month weekend robot programming certificate and uses AI tools more. Offers to train other operators on Friday afternoons and asks the union to push for paid training time.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, with an edge of guilt.
S1.quote: He's brilliant with his hands but he hates screens, he calls the AI 'the robot's cousin'.
S1.fieldNote: Karl moves first and sees opportunity, but frames it in collective terms: paid training and shared gains. His guilt about colleagues like Mo is real and specific. He would consider leaving for an automation firm but prefers to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's different. Two years is not enough for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for big public answers, a basic income, public ownership of some of this, something. I'd go to the demonstrations. I'd also be telling people to learn the tools now, today, because waiting is the worst option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still be okay for maybe a year longer than most, because I'd be the one setting up the robots. But if the AI can program the robots itself, my edge is a year, not a career. I keep coming back to that. My skills are good, but they're good at exactly the thing this replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to jump to a robot integrator firm in the first six months while they're desperate for people, and take the pay rise. I'd save every bit of that rise, aiming for six months of savings. I'd do some weekend setup work for small shops on the side, and I'd stay active in the union pushing for proper redundancy terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be moving, which helps. I'm worse when I'm sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your skills are good at exactly the thing this replaces. Say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'm proud of is turning a drawing into a program and a perfect part. That's literally what AGI plus a robot does. My dad laughed at me once for being the guy who reads manuals for fun. In this one, the manuals read themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're probably fine for a bit, which is true, and that I'm going to work like mad for a year, which is also true. She'd ask about her school. I wouldn't have an answer. Teachers might be okay longer, or not.

S2.say: He'd call for big public answers such as a basic income and public ownership, and join demonstrations. He'd urge people to learn AI tools immediately rather than wait.
S2.think: He thinks he'd stay employed perhaps a year longer than most by setting up robots, but sees his edge as short if AI can program robots itself. His proudest skill is exactly what this replaces.
S2.do: Moves to a robot integrator firm within six months for a pay rise and saves it towards six months of savings. Takes weekend setup work for small shops and stays active in the union on redundancy terms.
S2.feel: Anxious but steadied by keeping busy.
S2.quote: My dad laughed at me once for being the guy who reads manuals for fun. In this one, the manuals read themselves.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version is where Karl's confidence cracks: he sees his strength as the very thing being automated. He reacts by moving fast and earning while demand lasts, while calling for big public solutions. His politics and his personal plans pull in the same direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use these five years to set up the rules: who owns the robots, who gets the money. Online I'd be pushing for public retraining and a proper debate about a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is enough to be on the right side of it, at least for a while. I'd want to be one of the people designing the robot cells, not just running them. After 2031, I don't know. Nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot programming certificate in year one, then an evening course in automation engineering. I'd start a small side business with a mate, setting up cheap robot arms for local workshops, with maybe two thousand put in from savings. And I'd campaign for a party that wants workers to share in automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly busy and hopeful, but there's a 'then what' sitting at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that side business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small shops on our estate, the sign makers, the cabinet guy, can't afford the big integrators. A second-hand arm and a bit of programming could save them hours. I'd charge fair and do it on Saturdays. It's a way of making sure the little guys aren't left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that helping to automate other people's jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I've thought about that. Most of those shops are one or two people who are drowning in work, not firing anyone. But you're right, it's not clean. I'd rather be in the room and argue for fairness than sit outside it.

S3.say: He'd say the five years should be used to settle who owns robots and who benefits. Online he'd push for public retraining and a shorter working week.
S3.think: He believes five years is enough to end up designing robot cells rather than running them, at least for a while. He admits nobody knows what comes after 2031.
S3.do: Completes the robot programming certificate in year one, then an automation engineering evening course. Starts a Saturday side business with a friend installing cheap robot arms for small workshops, putting in about two thousand from savings, and campaigns for a party backing worker-shared automation.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy and mostly hopeful, with a lingering question about what follows.
S3.quote: I'd rather be in the room and argue for fairness than sit outside it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Karl turns into a builder, retraining and starting a small automation business for local workshops. He accepts the contradiction of automating others while campaigning for workers. His mood is lower than in the fast version because time lets him plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Probably at my peak, in theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we can get it right. Ten years is enough to set up worker co-ops, public ownership, retraining, all of it. I'd say that and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is more than enough for me to build a career around this. The question isn't me, it's what work even means by 2036. I'd want to own a piece of the machines, not just be paid to tend them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the automation engineering diploma over two or three years, part-time. With a few mates from the shop we'd look at setting up a small machining co-op, worker-owned, with robot cells, putting in savings over time. I'd keep campaigning and voting for policies that spread ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. The future is good for me, but I'm not sure it's good for everyone, and that sits with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-op rather than just your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the robots do the work, the money has to go somewhere. If the five of us own it, it goes to us and our families. If some investor owns it, it goes to him. That's my politics in one sentence, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in year nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan and Mo and the guys who didn't want to retrain. I'd have had ten years to bring them along. If I haven't, that's on me as much as anyone.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to get it right with worker co-ops, public ownership and retraining, and he'd mean it.
S4.think: He's confident he can build a career in a decade; his worry is what work means at all by 2036. He wants to own part of the machines rather than only tend them.
S4.do: Studies part-time for an automation engineering diploma over two to three years. Plans a worker-owned machining co-op with colleagues, investing savings over time, and keeps voting and campaigning for policies that spread ownership.
S4.feel: Uneasy: good prospects for himself but doubts it will be good for everyone.
S4.quote: If some investor owns it, it goes to him. That's my politics in one sentence, I suppose.
S4.fieldNote: Karl's long-horizon plan is a worker-owned co-op, which combines his progressive views with his appetite for technology. His unease is about others, not himself. He holds himself responsible for colleagues who don't retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything fair. Things done in a panic always end up with the people at the top keeping the money. What would help is a public retraining wage, so people can afford to learn, and rules that let workers own a share of the machines that replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the guys who hate screens. People like me get asked these questions because we sound interesting. Mo is the one who'd really need help, and he'd never fill in a survey.

headlineQuote: The thing I'm proud of is turning a drawing into a program and a perfect part. That's literally what AGI plus a robot does.
portrait: Karl Patel is twenty-seven, the senior operator on a five-axis CNC cell at an aerospace machine shop, living with his partner Leila, a primary teacher, on about three months of savings. He uses AI every day and moves early on new technology, but frames everything through progressive ideas about shared ownership. He is calm when AI fizzles and with steady change, where he plans a robot programming certificate. AGI in two years makes him anxious, because his proudest skill is what it replaces, and he would jump to an automation firm. With five or ten years he plans a side business and then a worker-owned co-op, worrying most about colleagues who won't retrain.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because panic leaves no time to build anything fair and the people at the top keep the money.
whatWouldHelp: A public retraining wage so people can afford to learn, and rules that let workers own a share of the machines that replace them.
